### SETUP CODE: Runs the whole model if it doesn't exist, else loads the results. Doesn't output anything and all debugging surpressed for this QMD.

import os
import sys
import pandas as pd
import hazelbean as hb

repo_root_candidates = [
    os.environ.get('GLOBAL_INVEST_REPO_ROOT'),
    os.getcwd(),
    os.path.join(os.path.expanduser('~'), 'Files', 'global_invest', 'global_invest_dev'),
]
for repo_root in repo_root_candidates:
    if repo_root and os.path.exists(os.path.join(repo_root, 'global_invest')):
        if repo_root not in sys.path:
            sys.path.insert(0, repo_root)
        break

from global_invest.coastal_carbon import coastal_carbon_initialization

if __name__ == '__main__':

    # ProjectFlow object
    p = hb.ProjectFlow()
    p.project_name = 'gep_coastal_carbon'
    p.project_dir = os.path.join(
        os.path.expanduser('~'), 'Files', 'global_invest', 'projects', p.project_name
    )
    p.base_data_dir = (
        "/Users/long/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-yxlong@umn.edu/"
        "Shared drives/NatCapTEEMs/Files/base_data/submissions"
    )
    p.set_project_dir(p.project_dir)

    # Task tree. Use the calculation-only tree here; the full tree includes
    # this Quarto render task and would recurse during report generation.
    coastal_carbon_initialization.build_gep_service_calculation_task_tree(p, include_seagrass=True)

    # Project level attributes - Data Paths

    # Country boundaries (marine EEZ)
    p.df_countries_marine_csv_path = p.get_path(
        'cartographic', 'ee', 'eemarine_r566_correspondence.csv'
    )
    p.gdf_countries_marine_vector_path = p.get_path(
        'cartographic', 'ee', 'eemarine_r566_correspondence.gpkg'
    )

    # Country boundaries (terrestrial r264). The CSV is consumed by
    # gep_calculation to collapse the r566 _EEZ Totals down to iso3_r250.
    p.df_countries_csv_path = p.get_path(
        'cartographic', 'ee', 'ee_r264_correspondence.csv'
    )
    p.gdf_countries_vector_path = p.get_path(
        'cartographic', 'ee', 'ee_r264_correspondence.gpkg'
    )
    p.gdf_countries_vector_simplified_path = p.get_path(
        'cartographic', 'ee', 'ee_r264_simplified30sec.gpkg'
    )

    # Mangrove data (Global Mangrove Watch v3)
    p.mangrove_vector_path = os.path.join(
        p.base_data_dir, 'coastal_carbon', 'gmw_v3_2019_vec', 'gmw_v3_2019_vec.shp'
    )

    # Salt marsh data (processed from GWL_FCS30D)
    p.salt_marsh_vector_path = os.path.join(
        p.base_data_dir, 'coastal_carbon', 'global_salt_marsh2019.gpkg'
    )

    # Seagrass extent (UNEP-WCMC013-014 SeagrassPtPy v7.1, polygon shapefile).
    p.seagrass_vector_path = os.path.join(
        p.base_data_dir, 'coastal_carbon',
        '014_001_WCMC013-014_SeagrassPtPy2021_v7_1', '01_Data',
        'WCMC013_014_Seagrasses_Py_v7_1.shp'
    )

    # Sanderman et al. 2018 mangrove SOC raster (top 1 m, Mg C/ha).
    p.mangrove_soc_path = os.path.join(
        p.base_data_dir, 'coastal_carbon',
        'soc.tha_tnc.mangroves.typology_m_30m_b0..100cm_2019_2020_go_epsg.4326_v1.2.tif'
    )

    # Optional: mean annual precipitation raster (mm/yr) for tropical wet/dry split.
    p.precipitation_path = os.path.join(
        p.base_data_dir, 'coastal_carbon', 'mean_annual_precipitation_mm.tif'
    )

    # Reference raster for area calculation (ha per cell)

# Introduction

Carbon storage in mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows is an essential coastal "blue carbon" ecosystem service for climate change mitigation [@mcleod2011; @howard2014; @ipcc2014; @macreadie2021] (@fig-ecosystems). Here we provide a comprehensive, global, country-level economic assessment of the carbon stock held in these three BCE types within the Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) framework. We focus on the standing stock of organic carbon contained within each coastal country's marine Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), following the country-level blue carbon natural-capital accounting framework of Bertram et al. [@bertram2021], and value that stock through the rental social cost of carbon.

display(Image(ecosystem_map_path))

Notes: This figure is plotted from the Global Mangrove Watch v3 [@bunting2018], the GLC_FCS30D salt marsh layer [@zhang2024] and the UNEP-WCMC Global Distribution of Seagrasses v7.1 [@unepwcmc2021]; the ecosystem-trio framing follows Macreadie et al. [@macreadie2021].


# Data and Methods

The spatial domain of this analysis is the marine Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) of each coastal country, which we treat as the coastal area attributed to that country, following the country-level blue-carbon natural-capital accounting framework of Bertram et al. [@bertram2021]. Restricting the domain to EEZs delineates the coastal-water envelope where mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass ecosystems occur, and, by construction, ensures that the coastal-carbon accounts reported here do not spatially overlap with the terrestrial-carbon service, which is reported on land within the standard terrestrial country boundaries.

## Data sources

Mangrove extent comes from the Global Mangrove Watch v3 vector product for 2019 [@bunting2018], which integrates ALOS PALSAR and Landsat observations to map mangrove forests at 30 m globally. Salt marsh extent is taken from a pre-processed vector layer extracted from the Zhang et al. GLC_FCS30D global land-cover product for 2019 [@zhang2024]. Seagrass extent comes from the UNEP-WCMC Global Distribution of Seagrasses v7.1 polygon product [@unepwcmc2021] (293,147 polygons globally), released in 2021 as a multi-year compilation of field observations spanning the late nineteenth century to 2018. No global wall-to-wall seagrass map exists for the 2019 base year used here, but seagrass meadows are slow-changing ecosystems whose extent persists on decadal timescales, so the WCMC v7.1 compilation is treated as the best available 2019 baseline. The area totals it produces sit within the high- to low-confidence global extent range of 160,000 to 267,000 km² synthesised by McKenzie et al. [@mckenzie2020] from the same underlying field record, which is the extent layer adopted by the most recent global seagrass blue-carbon synthesis [@gomis2025]; in other words, WCMC v7.1 is the polygon-level realisation of the same observational record that McKenzie and Gomis use in tabular form.

Mangrove soil organic carbon is taken from the Sanderman et al. random-forest map of mangrove soil organic carbon at 30 m, top 1 m depth [@sanderman2018]. We use the median-typology product for the 2019 to 2020 epoch; the file is reprojected once onto the 10 arc-second grid using average resampling and cached on disk for subsequent runs. Salt marsh soil carbon is taken from a latitude step function summarizing the Maxwell et al. MarSOC synthesis [@maxwell2024], with values rising from ~180 Mg C/ha in the tropics to ~350 Mg C/ha at high latitudes. Seagrass soil carbon is set to a Fourqurean et al. [@fourqurean2012] global mean of 22 Mg C/ha for the top 20 cm, scaled to ~70 Mg C/ha for the top 1 m to align with the soil-depth convention used for mangrove and salt marsh; the scalar assumes a roughly linear depth profile and is a known approximation that the source dataset does not directly support.

## Quantifying the blue carbon stock

The country-level storage value is built from a quantity step and a pricing step. The quantity step, described in this subsection, estimates the standing organic carbon stock in each coastal country's EEZ; the pricing step, described in the following subsection, converts that stock into an annualised monetary value. For each ecosystem the per-pixel (or per-polygon, for seagrass) carbon stock is the sum of above-ground biomass carbon, below-ground biomass carbon and soil organic carbon to 1 m depth, each term drawn from the published global product appropriate to that ecosystem.

### Mangroves

Above-ground biomass density is computed from the Hamilton and Friess [@hamilton2018] combined latitude regression, $AGB = \max(0,\, -6.4305\,|\text{lat}| + 271.747)$ in tonnes per hectare, which averages the earlier Twilley et al. [@twilley1992] and Saenger and Snedaker [@saenger1993] equations and explains roughly four times more variance than any single prior latitude-only model. AGB is converted to carbon at 0.48 following Hamilton and Friess [@hamilton2018].

Below-ground biomass is allocated from AGB using the IPCC [@ipcc2014] Wetlands Supplement Table 4.6 climate-zone ratios, in line with the recent Wang et al. mangrove storage map [@wang2025]. Tropical wet pixels (`|lat| < 23.5°` and mean annual precipitation greater than 2,000 mm) use a BGB:AGB ratio of 0.49; tropical dry pixels (same latitude range, lower precipitation) use 0.29; and subtropical pixels (`|lat| ≥ 23.5°`) use 0.96. When no precipitation raster is configured, all tropical pixels default to the wet-tropical ratio, which is the dominant condition for global mangroves but slightly overestimates BGB along the Arabian and Australian dry-tropical coasts. BGB is converted to carbon at 0.39 following Howard et al. [@howard2014].

Soil organic carbon is read directly from the Sanderman map at the pixel scale, with no further parameterisation. As a fallback when the Sanderman raster is not available locally, the pipeline reverts to a latitude step function (decreasing from 400 Mg C/ha at the equator to 250 Mg C/ha by 25° latitude) that approximates the Sanderman global mean. Total mangrove ecosystem carbon at a tropical wet equatorial pixel with Sanderman SOC = 400 Mg C/ha is therefore approximately 130 + 52 + 400 ≈ 582 Mg C/ha, consistent with the upper end of the Macreadie et al. published range [@macreadie2021] for equatorial mangroves.

### Salt marshes

Above-ground biomass for salt marshes is set to a Chmura et al. global median of 5 t/ha [@chmura2003], boosted by a factor of 1.2 in tropical pixels (`|lat| < 25°`) to reflect higher productivity in warm, perennially flooded settings. The conservative 2.5 below-ground to above-ground ratio captures the marsh root systems' large allocation to below-ground biomass, which sits within the published 2:1 to 5:1 range. Biomass is converted to carbon at 0.45 (AGB) and 0.41 (BGB) following Howard et al. [@howard2014].

Soil organic carbon is read from a four-bin latitude step function calibrated against the Maxwell et al. MarSOC synthesis [@maxwell2024]: 180 Mg C/ha in the tropics, rising through 220 Mg C/ha in the warm temperate zone and 250 Mg C/ha in the cool temperate zone, to 350 Mg C/ha in peat-rich boreal and arctic marshes. A native MarSOC raster is not currently wired into the pipeline; the step function captures the latitudinal first order but not the substantial within-zone variability documented in the source dataset.

A representative salt marsh pixel at 30°N with median productivity and 220 Mg C/ha soil carbon yields approximately 7 + 220 ≈ 227 Mg C/ha total, reflecting the marsh's near-total reliance on soil for storage.

### Seagrasses

Above- and below-ground biomass carbon densities are assigned per polygon using the genus-specific means from Gomis, Strydom, Foster et al. [@gomis2025], who report total biomass carbon densities spanning roughly two orders of magnitude across the twelve genera in the global database: 9.78 Mg C/ha for *Posidonia* (the highest), ~3.70 Mg C/ha for other persistent genera (*Phyllospadix*, *Enhalus*, *Cymodocea*, *Thalassia*, *Amphibolis*, *Thalassodendron*), ~0.94 Mg C/ha for opportunistic genera (*Zostera*, *Syringodium*, *Halodule*), 0.33 Mg C/ha for *Ruppia* and 0.19 Mg C/ha for *Halophila*. Polygons with no genus identification (≈78 percent of the WCMC dataset) receive the Gomis 2025 global mean of 1.55 Mg C/ha. The total biomass density is split 30 percent above-ground and 70 percent below-ground in line with the seagrass-wide finding that root and rhizome systems dominate biomass [@howard2014; @fourqurean2012]. Polygons whose genus is a freshwater plant (*Trapa*, *Myriophyllum*, *Valisneria*, *Najas*, *Heteranthera*, *Stuckenia*, *Utricularia*) are zeroed out before aggregation.

Soil organic carbon is set to a constant 70 Mg C/ha for the top 1 m, derived by scaling the Fourqurean et al. [@fourqurean2012] top 20 cm value of 22 Mg C/ha. This is the same uniform constant for every polygon; spatial heterogeneity is currently not captured, and adding a native MarSOC-style raster for seagrass would be a natural future improvement. Per-polygon stock is the density times the polygon area in hectares, computed in the EPSG:6933 equal-area projection after intersection with the country EEZ polygons.


## Pricing the carbon stock with the rental SCC

To estimate the value of carbon storage and sequestration, we use the rental social cost of carbon (SCC) [@parisa2022; @groom2023; @venmans2025] as the pricing metric. Parisa et al. [@parisa2022] provide the theoretical rationale for quantifying the value of short-term carbon storage, which corresponds to carbon storage and sequestration. Following this approach, and within the Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) framework, we estimate the annual rental value of carbon storage as

$$
\text{rental SCC}(t) = P_C(t) - P_C(t+1)\,e^{-r} = P_C(t) - P_C(t)\,e^{g}\,e^{-r} = P_C(t)\,\bigl(1 - e^{-x}\bigr),
$$

where $P_C(t)$ is the social cost of carbon in year $t$, $P_C(t+1)$ is the social cost of carbon in year $t+1$, $r$ is the discount rate, $g$ is the rate of growth of the social cost of carbon, and $x = r - g$ is the net carbon discount rate. The rental valuation measures the annualised benefit of temporarily storing one metric tonne of CO₂ for one year. The country-level storage value is the product of the in-country carbon stock, this rental price and a natural contribution ratio of 1,

$$
GEP_{\text{coastal carbon}} = C_{\text{total}} \times \text{rental SCC} \times 1.
$$

Because our base year is 2019, computing the one-year rental rate requires $P_C(2019)$ and $P_C(2020)$. The Greenhouse gas Impact Value Estimator (GIVE) model's damage functions begin in 2020, making direct computation of $P_C(2019)$ infeasible. We use the GIVE model because it represents the current state of the art in SCC estimation, integrating four sectoral damage channels (mortality, agriculture, energy and sea level rise) with probabilistic socioeconomic projections from the Resources for the Future Socioeconomic Pathways (RFF-SPs), and forms the basis of the updated U.S. EPA social cost of carbon [@rennert2022]. We therefore approximate $P_C(2019)$ using $P_C(2020)$. This approximation is justified on two grounds. First, the year-over-year growth rate of the SCC is modest: our replication shows approximately 1.6% growth from 2020 to 2021 (from \$185 to \$188 per tCO₂ at the 2.0\% Ramsey rate), driven primarily by GDP growth and cumulative emissions. Second, the COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp contraction in global GDP in 2020 which would have compressed the difference between the 2019 and 2020 SCCs. Together, the small baseline growth rate and the recessionary shock in 2020 imply that $P_C(2019)$ and $P_C(2020)$ are nearly identical.

Under this approximation, we adopt a carbon price of \$678.33 per metric tonne of carbon (tC), corresponding to the mean SCC estimated by Rennert et al. [@rennert2022] at a 2% discount rate, converted from CO₂ to carbon units (\$185.05/tCO₂ × 3.664 tCO₂/tC). The resulting annual rental rate is approximately \$13.43 per tC in 2020 US dollars. To express this in constant 2019 dollars we adjust for inflation using the GDP deflator reported by the World Bank as 1.85% for 2019, giving \$13.43 / 1.0185 ≈ \$13.19 per tC in 2019 US dollars. The same rental price is applied to mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass stocks, treating each tonne of carbon as fungible across ecosystems.

Across the four candidate Ramsey discount rates considered here (1.5%, 2.0%, 2.5%, 3.0%), the inflation-adjusted rental SCC in 2019 dollars ranges from \$8.51 per tC at a 3.0% discount rate to \$16.50 per tC at a 1.5% discount rate, with the 2.0% baseline used in this study sitting near the middle of this range at \$13.19 per tC. @tbl-rental-scc-discount summarizes the rental price at these four rates; the 2.0% row is the baseline used in this study.

| Discount rate | Growth rate (carbon price) | Net discount rate (discount rate − growth rate) | SC-CO₂ (2020\$) | SCC (2020\$) | Rental SCC (2020\$) | Rental SCC (2019\$) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.015 | 0 | 0.015 | 308 | 1,129.33 | 16.81 | 16.50 |
| **0.020** | **0** | **0.020** | **185** | **678.33** | **13.43** | **13.19** |
| 0.025 | 0 | 0.025 | 118 | 432.67 | 10.68 | 10.49 |
| 0.030 | 0 | 0.030 | 80 | 293.33 | 8.67 | 8.51 |

: Rental social cost of carbon at alternative Ramsey discount rates. {#tbl-rental-scc-discount}

# Results

Coastal blue carbon storage generates a gross economic product of approximately \$`{python} f"{total_coastal_carbon_value/1e9:,.2f}"` billion (2019$) in the base year. The account covers `{python} f"{total_eez_area_mha:,.1f}"` million hectares of mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass habitat inside national EEZs, storing `{python} f"{total_eez_stock_pg:,.2f}"` Pg C valued at the baseline rental SCC of \$13.19 per tC.

Seagrass dominates the global value because the mapped seagrass extent is large and the 1 m soil-carbon constant applies across that extent. Mangroves have the highest per-hectare stocks but a smaller EEZ-area footprint in the final country account, while salt marshes contribute a mid-sized share from temperate and high-latitude coastlines.

```{python}

```

Because the country-level storage value scales linearly with the rental price, the global blue carbon storage value implied by the discount-rate range in @tbl-rental-scc-discount is approximately \$`{python} f"{total_coastal_carbon_value/1e9*8.51/13.19:,.2f}"` billion at a 3.0% rate and \$`{python} f"{total_coastal_carbon_value/1e9*16.50/13.19:,.2f}"` billion at a 1.5% rate.

# Validation

We validate the coastal-carbon results in two steps. First, we compare the monetary value of the global account against Bertram et al. [@bertram2021], who provide the closest published global country-level economic assessment of blue carbon wealth. Second, we compare the physical carbon-stock totals produced by the pipeline against ecosystem-specific published estimates for mangroves, salt marshes and seagrasses.

Bertram et al. [@bertram2021] find that global blue carbon wealth generated by carbon sequestration in coastal blue carbon ecosystems amounts to US$190.7 ± 29.5 billion yr^-1^, based on a global mean SCC of US$640.3 ± 4.93 tCO~2~^-1^. Our baseline estimate is US$`{python} f"{total_coastal_carbon_value/1e9:,.2f}"` billion yr^-1^ in 2019 dollars, based on an SC-CO~2~ of US$185.05 tCO~2~^-1^ and an annual rental SCC of US$13.19 tC^-1^. The lower value is therefore expected: Bertram et al. apply a substantially higher full SCC to annual carbon sequestration, while this study focuses on the annual rental value of standing carbon stock within each country's EEZ. The two estimates therefore differ both in valuation parameter and in the physical quantity being valued: annual sequestration in Bertram et al., and stored carbon stock here.

After this economic validation, we compare the physical stock estimates by ecosystem. Differences reflect (i) the extent layer chosen (GMW v3 2019 for mangroves; pre-processed GLC_FCS30D 2019 for salt marshes; WCMC v7.1 compilation for seagrass), (ii) the soil-depth convention (top 1 m throughout, sometimes deeper in field studies) and (iii) the per-pixel density product (Sanderman 2018 raster for mangrove SOC; latitude-step functions for salt marsh SOC and Fourqurean-scaled constant for seagrass SOC).

## Mangrove

The pipeline produces a global mangrove total of **11.75 Pg C** over the GMW v3 2019 extent (~14.7 Mha), decomposed in @tbl-validate-mangrove.

| Component | This study (Pg C) | Published (Pg C) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Above-ground biomass C | 2.81 | 1.5 – 3.0 | Hamilton & Friess [@hamilton2018]; Hutchison [@hutchison2014]; Simard [@simard2019] |
| Below-ground biomass C | 1.15 | 0.7 – 1.5 | IPCC Wetlands Supplement ratios [@ipcc2014] |
| Soil organic C, top 1 m | 7.79 | 6.4 | Sanderman [@sanderman2018] |
| Total ecosystem C | 11.75 | 5.72 ± 0.10 (2020, 13.6 Mha) ; 8.05 (2000, 6.2 Mha) | Ju [@ju2025]; Wang [@wang2025] |

: Global mangrove carbon stock, this study vs published estimates. {#tbl-validate-mangrove}

Our mangrove SOC total (7.79 Pg C) is roughly 20 percent above the Sanderman et al. global figure of 6.4 Pg C [@sanderman2018], because the all-touched rasterisation of GMW v3 onto the 10 arc-second grid retains thin coastal fringes that the original 30 m Sanderman product does not, expanding the integrated extent. Our above-ground biomass (2.81 Pg C) sits at the upper end of the published range and is consistent with the Hamilton and Friess latitude regression [@hamilton2018] over the broader GMW v3 extent. Our total (11.75 Pg C) is therefore higher than Ju et al. [@ju2025] and Wang et al. [@wang2025], a difference that is driven primarily by extent (we use a recent and inclusive extent layer) and only secondarily by the density products.

## Salt marsh

The pipeline produces a global salt marsh total of **4.04 Pg C** over the GLC_FCS30D 2019 extent, decomposed in @tbl-validate-saltmarsh.

| Component | This study (Pg C) | Published (Pg C) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Above-ground biomass C | 0.038 | 0.03 – 0.05 | Chmura [@chmura2003] |
| Below-ground biomass C | 0.086 | 0.07 – 0.15 | Howard manual ratios [@howard2014] |
| Soil organic C, top 1 m | 3.92 | 1.4 – 2.1 (MarSOC) ; 0.4 (McLeod 2011 review) | Maxwell [@maxwell2024]; McLeod [@mcleod2011] |
| Total ecosystem C | 4.04 | 1.5 – 2.1 | Maxwell [@maxwell2024] |

: Global salt marsh carbon stock, this study vs published estimates. {#tbl-validate-saltmarsh}

Our salt marsh SOC (3.92 Pg C) is roughly twice the Maxwell et al. MarSOC global estimate of 1.4 – 2.1 Pg C [@maxwell2024]. The principal driver is the latitude step function used here, which assigns 180 – 350 Mg C/ha across latitude bands; Maxwell et al. report a global area-weighted mean of ~225 Mg C/ha and a more conservative global extent. Replacing the step function with the native MarSOC raster would bring our salt marsh total back toward the Maxwell range, and is the most consequential improvement remaining in the pipeline for this ecosystem.

## Seagrass

The pipeline produces a global seagrass total of **4.82 Pg C** over the WCMC v7.1 extent (~16 – 27 Mha, McKenzie 2020 confidence range), decomposed in @tbl-validate-seagrass.

| Component | This study (Pg C) | Published (Pg C) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Above-ground biomass C | 0.046 | 0.007 – 0.012 | Gomis [@gomis2025] |
| Below-ground biomass C | 0.107 | 0.017 – 0.028 | Gomis [@gomis2025] |
| Total biomass C | 0.153 | 0.024 – 0.040 | Gomis [@gomis2025] |
| Soil organic C, top 1 m | 4.67 | 4.2 – 8.4 | Fourqurean [@fourqurean2012]; Macreadie [@macreadie2021] |
| Total ecosystem C | 4.82 | 4.3 – 8.4 | Fourqurean [@fourqurean2012] |

: Global seagrass carbon stock, this study vs published estimates. {#tbl-validate-seagrass}

Our seagrass biomass-only total (0.153 Pg C) is roughly four to six times the Gomis et al. 2025 range of 0.024 – 0.040 Pg C [@gomis2025] because (i) ~78 percent of WCMC polygons receive the Gomis global mean of 1.55 Mg C/ha when their genus is not identified, which is conservative for stocks but generous when applied over the full WCMC extent rather than the McKenzie high-confidence subset, and (ii) the WCMC v7.1 extent of ~27 Mha is at the upper end of the published range. Our soil total (4.67 Pg C) sits within the Fourqurean 2012 lower bound, because the 70 Mg C/ha top-1 m constant is itself a conservative scaling of the Fourqurean top-20 cm mean.

# Conclusion

We provide a country-level economic assessment of coastal blue carbon storage across marine EEZs, combining recent extent and density products for mangroves, salt marshes and seagrasses with the rental social cost of carbon at a 2 percent Ramsey discount rate. The approach extends the country-level blue carbon natural-capital framework of Bertram et al. [@bertram2021] from the annual sequestration flow to the standing-stock storage component, and aligns with the IPCC Tier 1 conventions for wetland carbon accounting [@ipcc2014].

The methodology is deliberately conservative on three axes. Soil depth is fixed at 1 m, in line with the IPCC Tier 1 convention [@ipcc2014] and with recent global stock-mapping efforts [@sanderman2018; @ju2025; @wang2025], although mangrove peats often extend to 2 m or beyond [@donato2011]. Mangrove above-ground biomass is taken from the Hamilton and Friess latitude regression [@hamilton2018] rather than canopy-height or bioclimatic models [@hutchison2014; @simard2019], trading some local accuracy for global parsimony. Tropical-wet versus tropical-dry below-ground allocation is latitude-only when no precipitation raster is configured; supplying mean annual precipitation refines this and improves estimates in dry-tropical mangroves of Saudi Arabia, Senegal and northern Australia.

Seagrass storage remains the weakest of the three ecosystems. The biomass component is genus-aware, but ≈78 percent of WCMC polygons lack a genus identification and the soil component is a uniform global constant rather than a spatial product. Future work should ingest a gridded seagrass SOC layer, no published equivalent of Sanderman 2018 or Maxwell 2024 exists at present, and split the global mean across bioregions, where the Mediterranean averages roughly 50 percent above the global mean [@gomis2025].
